comparison: Perfect alignment on background claims C2-C6. Both evaluations find these literature-based contextual claims supported. OpenEval emphasizes appropriate attribution to prior work, while peer reviewers implicitly accept the framing as solid.

Strong agreement on core empirical findings (C11-C20, C65-C76). Both find the statistical evidence solid. Peer review R1 also includes sensitivity analyses (C21-C23) and comparative claims (C24-C27, C29-C30) that OpenEval separates into R4, R5, and R6, but all are marked as supported by both evaluators.

OpenEval separately evaluates sensitivity analyses (C21-C23) as supported, noting appropriate handling of confounders. Peer reviewers group these with main findings in R1, affirming the overall message about abandonment at writing stage.

OpenEval evaluates comparative claims across omics technologies (C24-C28) separately. Peer review R1 includes C24-C27 with main findings, while C28 appears in peer R7. Both find claims supported, though organized differently.

OpenEval separately evaluates synthesis claims about reporting vs citing articles (C29-C30). Peer reviewers include these in R1 with main findings. Both agree these claims are well-supported by the data.

Strong agreement on citation analysis findings (C31-C34, C78). Both find the statistical evidence solid and the contradiction of the citation-avoidance hypothesis well-supported. Peer R2 also includes subgroup analyses (C35-C42) that OpenEval separates into R8 and R9.

OpenEval separately evaluates subgroup analyses by disease and technique (C35-C40). Peer reviewers group these with main citation findings in R2. Both find the evidence solid and accept the consistency across categories.

OpenEval separately evaluates the exception for high-throughput techniques (C41-C42). Peer reviewers include these in R2 with citation analysis. Both find claims supported, with OpenEval noting appropriate framing as inference.

Strong agreement on factor analysis (C43-C48). Both find the systematic identification of 45 factors and statistical associations well-supported. Peer R3 also includes correlation analysis (C49-C51) that OpenEval separates into R11.
OpenEval separately evaluates correlation patterns among factors (C49-C51). Peer reviewers group these with main factor analysis in R3. Both find the cluster analysis appropriately documented.
OpenEval separately evaluates tool availability claim (C52). Peer reviewers include this with case study in R4. Both find the resource description acceptable.

Strong agreement on case study demonstrating FMUG utility (C53-C59). Both find the hypothesis-to-validation story compelling. Peer R4 also includes literature review (C60-C63) and impact claim (C84) that OpenEval separates into R14 and R17.

OpenEval separately evaluates systematic literature review results (C60-C63). Peer reviewers group these with case study in R4. Both find the percentages clearly stated and supportive of the tool's value.

OpenEval evaluates data sources and filtering criteria (C7-C10, C64) as supported methodological statements. Peer R6 groups these with other methods (C77, C79-C83), accepting the overall analytical framework.
OpenEval separately evaluates differential expression threshold (C77). Peer reviewers include this with methodological claims in R6. Both find the threshold standard and appropriate.

OpenEval evaluates limitation acknowledgments (C79-C83) as appropriately qualifying results. Peer reviewers include these with methods in R6, accepting the overall approach after revisions addressed concerns.

Divergence in evaluation type. OpenEval marks future-looking claims (C84-C86) as UNCERTAIN due to speculation beyond the case study. Peer reviewers mark these as SUPPORTED in R7, implicitly accepting them as reasonable implications. OpenEval is more conservative about speculative claims.

OpenEval groups impact belief (C84) with other speculative claims (C85-C86) and marks as UNCERTAIN. Peer reviewers include C84 with case study in R4 and mark as SUPPORTED, viewing it as demonstrated by the Sfpq example.

OpenEval includes GWAS correlation explanation (C28) with comparative omics claims in R5, marking as supported. Peer reviewers group C28 with forward-looking implications in R7. Both find it acceptable, though categorized differently.
